newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan president pledges heavy sugar import taxes.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan president pledges heavy sugar import taxes.

text.p: Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi has pledged "heavy taxes" on sugar imports to protect the local industry against what he described as unfair competition.
Moi told a Labour Day rally in Nairobi on Thursday sugar was imported on the pretext that it was for Kenya's neighbours but then sold locally.

"Such importations are breaking the spirit of workers since the country is in a position to produce enough sugar to meet local demand," Moi said, adding that production of most imported sugar was subsidized and evasion of taxes meant that it then posed very unfair competition to local produce.
Moi said "heavy taxes would be a solution to that".

In January, retail and wholsesale sugar prices saw marginal fluctuations from December. The average ex-factory prices were 1,850 and 3,700 Kenyan shillings ($34.9 to $69.81) for 50 kg (110 lb) and 100 kg respectively.
Imported sugar is available in local supermarkets at a wholesale price six percent lower than local sugar.

According to official Kenya Sugar Authority (KSA) figures, sugar imports totalled 65,826 tonnes in 1996 compared to 24,440 in 1995. But shipping sources said as much as 200,000 tonnes, mostly labelled as being in transit, ended up on the Kenyan market.

Neither the finance nor agriculture ministry would say what new taxes were envisaged. But previously, Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi has said it was not taxes that posed a major problem to local produce but corruption at the port that ensured taxes were not paid.

For the past two years, Kenya has levied six percent Value Added Tax (VAT) on imports, a sugar development levy of 20 percent, a blanket 25 percent duty and a variable dumping duty of $105.83 per tonne of imported sugar.
The finance ministry says tariffs and duties on imports had the effect of raising prices above domestic levels.
The KSA, citing drought and illegal imports into the local market, last week forecast slight growth in 1997 output to 400,000 tonnes from 386,000 last year.

"Imported sugar that has illegally found its way into the Kenyan market has also meant that there are high stocks held by sugar mills, which discourages them from raising capacity," said a KSA executive.

Sugar production remains well below consumption and industry experts say imports would remain a major source to meet the shortfall. Consumption is forecast to rise to 600,000 tonnes in 1997 from 560,000 in 1996.
